# Automorphisms of Rational Surfaces and Finite Abelian Subgroups of the Cremona Group

This article provides complete proofs for results that were previously announced in a 2007 note, and it presents a detailed study of the automorphisms of rational surfaces. Building on the earlier announcement, the present work develops the necessary machinery to establish these results rigorously and to place them within a broader geometric context.

A central contribution of this article is the establishment of a method for determining whether a given finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group of the plane is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal surface. This criterion offers a practical and systematic approach to a fundamental question in the theory of birational transformations, allowing one to decide when such a subgroup can be realised, up to conjugacy, as genuine automorphisms of a well-behaved surface.

Among the principal results, we show that a finite cyclic group of birational plane transformations is linearisable if and only if none of its non-trivial elements fixes a curve of positive genus. This provides a clean and intuitive characterisation of linearisability in the cyclic case, framed entirely in terms of the invariant curves associated with the group's elements.

The situation for finite Abelian groups is largely analogous, but with one notable subtlety. There exists a single exceptional case, corresponding to a group isomorphic to Z/2Z × Z/4Z, whose non-trivial elements fix no curve of positive genus and yet which is nonetheless not conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface. This exception highlights the delicate nature of the classification and underscores that the criterion valid in the cyclic case does not extend without modification to all Abelian groups.

Finally, the article offers descriptions of automorphisms—not necessarily of finite order—of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles. These descriptions complement the main classification results and provide additional insight into the structure of automorphism groups of rational surfaces, thereby situating the finite Abelian case within the wider landscape of surface automorphisms.

# Finite Abelian Subgroups of the Plane Cremona Group

## Introduction

The plane Cremona group, denoted $\mathrm{Cr}_2(k)$, consists of all birational transformations of the projective plane over a field $k$. Understanding its finite subgroups—and classifying them up to conjugacy—has been a central problem in algebraic geometry since the work of the Italian school. This article establishes rigorous proofs of results that had previously been announced, focusing specifically on finite Abelian subgroups and their conjugacy classes.

The principal contribution is the development of a systematic method for determining whether a given finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms acting on a minimal surface. This reduction is fundamental: rather than studying transformations of the plane in their full generality, one seeks a "nice" model—a minimal rational surface—on which the group acts by genuine automorphisms rather than birational maps.

## The Geometric Framework

By the equivariant version of the minimal model program, any finite subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(k)$ can be realized as a group of automorphisms of a rational surface $X$ that is $G$-minimal. Such a surface falls into one of two families:

- **Del Pezzo surfaces**, characterized by an ample anticanonical divisor, and
- **Conic bundles**, admitting a $G$-equivariant fibration whose fibers are conics.

Consequently, a complete understanding of finite group actions requires a careful description of the automorphisms of these two classes of surfaces. This article accordingly devotes substantial attention to cataloguing the possible automorphisms of del Pezzo surfaces of each degree, as well as those preserving conic bundle structures, together with the invariants that distinguish inequivalent actions.

## Linearisability and the Main Criterion

A finite subgroup is called **linearisable** if it is birationally conjugate to a subgroup of $\mathrm{PGL}_3(k)$—that is, to a group of *linear* projective transformations of $\mathbb{P}^2$. Linearisability is the simplest possible behavior, and identifying which groups possess this property is a natural goal.

The central result concerns cyclic groups. It establishes the following clean criterion:

> A finite cyclic subgroup of the Cremona group is linearisable **if and only if** no non-trivial element of the group fixes (pointwise) a curve of positive genus.

The geometric intuition behind this statement is compelling. The presence of a non-trivial element fixing a curve of genus $g \geq 1$ produces a birational invariant that obstructs any conjugation to a linear action, since linear automorphisms of the plane can only fix rational curves (lines and conics have genus zero). Conversely, in the absence of such an obstruction, one can always simplify the action down to the linear model.

## The Exceptional Abelian Group

While the genus criterion governs cyclic groups completely, its extension to general finite Abelian groups is *nearly* but not entirely valid. The article identifies a single, striking exception: there exists one group isomorphic to
$$
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}
$$
that violates the criterion. This particular group satisfies the condition that no non-trivial element fixes a curve of positive genus, yet it nevertheless fails to be linearisable.

This exception is significant precisely because it demonstrates that the elegant fixed-curve criterion, so powerful in the cyclic case, cannot be transferred verbatim to the Abelian setting. The obstruction to linearisability for this group is of a subtler nature, arising from the global structure of the action rather than from any single non-trivial element. Its existence marks the boundary of the naive generalization and underscores the additional care required in the classification of non-cyclic Abelian subgroups.

## Conclusion

By combining the minimal model reduction, an explicit analysis of automorphisms of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles, and the fixed-curve genus criterion, this work provides a comprehensive treatment of finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group. The results confirm the previously announced classification while highlighting, through the exceptional $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ group, the delicate ways in which birational rigidity can manifest beyond the reach of simple numerical invariants.

# Reflections on the Finite

This is a meditation on limits, on the edges where things end. We often imagine the world as boundless, yet nearly everything we touch is finite—measurable, countable, bound by beginnings and conclusions.

Consider Mont Blanc, the "white mountain" whose name comes from the French word *Blanc*. It rises as the highest peak in the Alps, a monument of stone and ice that seems eternal. Yet even this colossus is finite. Its glaciers retreat year by year, its snowpack thins, and geologists remind us that mountains, too, are temporary features on the shifting surface of the Earth. What appears permanent is simply changing slowly enough that a single human lifetime cannot perceive its end.

This tension between the apparent infinite and the actual finite runs through much of our thinking. A blank page—*blanc* in its purest sense—suggests endless possibility. But the words we write upon it are always finite, chosen from a limited vocabulary, arranged in sentences that must eventually stop. Even language, that seemingly boundless tool, operates within finite structures.

Mathematics offers the clearest illustration. A finite set can be counted; its members reach a definite total. This simplicity is comforting. Yet mathematicians also work with the infinite, and understanding the difference between the two has reshaped our entire conception of quantity, space, and time.

Perhaps this is the lesson: to recognize the finite is not to diminish the world but to appreciate it. Because things end—because Mont Blanc will not stand forever, because the blank page fills, because each moment passes—we learn to value what we have while we hold it.

# Abstract

We study finite abelian subgroups of the Cremona group $\mathrm{Cr}_2(k)$ of birational transformations of the projective plane over an algebraically closed field $k$. Building on the classical theory of Manin and Iskovskikh, we exploit the connection between conjugacy classes of finite subgroups and automorphisms of rational surfaces, realizing each such subgroup as a group of biregular automorphisms of a smooth rational surface $X$ acting minimally on a relatively minimal model. Our main results provide a complete classification, up to conjugacy, of the finite abelian subgroups arising from automorphisms of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.

For a finite abelian group $G$ acting faithfully on a rational surface, we analyze the induced action on the Picard lattice and the associated root system, using lattice-theoretic invariants and the equivariant Mori theory to distinguish conjugacy classes. We determine precisely which abelian groups embed into $\mathrm{Cr}_2(k)$, giving explicit generators and normal forms, and we compute the number of conjugacy classes in terms of the fixed-point data and the eigenvalue configurations on the anticanonical system. Particular attention is paid to groups acting with isolated fixed points, where we relate the local linearization to the global geometry of the invariant anticanonical curve.

As an application, we recover and extend known results on cyclic and $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2$ subgroups, describe the moduli of surfaces admitting a given abelian symmetry, and discuss consequences for the structure of the Cremona group, including rigidity phenomena and the failure of conjugacy for groups sharing the same abstract isomorphism type. We conclude with remarks on the positive-characteristic case and open questions concerning higher-dimensional analogues.

# Summary: Conjugacy of Finite Abelian Groups in the Cremona Group

## Overview

This research area concerns the classification of finite abelian subgroups of the **Cremona group** Cr₂(k)—the group of birational transformations of the projective plane. The central problem is determining when two such subgroups are **conjugate** within the Cremona group, a question rooted in the classical study of birational automorphisms initiated by Bertini, Kantor, and Wiman.

## Key Framework

The modern approach reduces conjugacy questions to the study of **regularized actions** on rational surfaces. By the theory of minimal models, any finite group acting birationally on ℙ² can be regularized so that the group acts by automorphisms on a smooth rational surface admitting a **G-equivariant Mori fibration**. This yields two fundamental cases:

1. **Del Pezzo surfaces** — where the surface has ample anticanonical class and Picard rank 1 (relative to the group action).
2. **Conic bundles** — where the surface fibers over ℙ¹ with rational curves as fibers.

## Main Themes

**Del Pezzo surface automorphisms:** Finite abelian groups acting on del Pezzo surfaces of varying degree are classified through their action on the Picard lattice and the configuration of exceptional curves. The Weyl group symmetries associated with each degree constrain the possible group structures.

**Conic bundle automorphisms:** For abelian groups preserving a conic bundle structure, the analysis focuses on the action on the base ℙ¹ and on the singular fibers. Invariants include the number and configuration of **degenerate fibers** and the induced permutation representations.

**Conjugacy invariants:** The classification distinguishes genuine conjugacy classes using birational invariants such as:
- Fixed-point loci and their geometry (e.g., fixed curves of positive genus),
- The **normalized fixed curves** and associated moduli,
- Lattice-theoretic data attached to the action.

## Significance

The results complete or refine the classification of finite abelian subgroups of Cr₂(k) up to conjugacy, extending the foundational work of Dolgachev–Iskovskikh. They clarify which abstract abelian groups embed into the Cremona group and enumerate the distinct geometric realizations, providing a bridge between birational geometry, lattice theory, and the theory of algebraic group actions.
